subtitle: Get more from advisory councils by making their input useful before a decision is made. Afterward, you will show accountability for how that input was used.
scope: For leaders who prepare decisions for advisory councils. Read the particular council’s law, charter, and procedures with its responsible staff. Advice does not itself confer decision authority. Matters involving Native American communities or Tribal relations should be referred to the person or area responsible within ADSA.
introTranscript: A council can help a team see effects it could not see alone. Its members need a real question, understandable preparation, a fair discussion, and a response that explains what changed. This course follows a practice service-notice decision through those steps. You will distinguish advice from authority, retain disagreement honestly, protect individual information, and review whether the advice reached the decision in time. Meeting counts and expressions of gratitude cannot replace meaningful influence and follow-through.

lessons.title: Give advice a real choice
lessons.summary: Distinguish the council’s remit from final decision authority.

intro.heading: Give advice a real choice
intro.body:
“What do you think?” can leave members guessing whether they should edit wording, reconsider policy, or endorse a finished decision. Start with the council’s remit and the actual choice. Explain who decides and what remains open.

In a practice service notice, an authorized review date may be fixed while contact methods and explanations remain undecided. Ask which outreach approach reduces confusion and what the team has overlooked. Do not imply the council can reverse a decision outside its authority.

A question outside the remit needs a different route. Members can identify a concern without being assigned new powers. Honest boundaries protect both useful advice and the council’s time.

flashcards.back: The council’s defined purpose and scope.
An opportunity to offer advice, distinct from final decision authority.
A clear question with alternatives, constraints, and missing evidence.
An important difference that should not be rewritten as consensus.
What the advice changed, what it did not, why, and what happens next.

items.title: Remit
items.body: A council’s authority comes from its governing arrangements, not from a facilitator’s invitation. In the notice case, check whether the council can recommend communication improvements before asking it to approve policy. This avoids spending members’ time on a power they do not hold.

items.title: Open choice
items.body: Make a two-column list of fixed requirements and open implementation choices. A fixed review date does not settle how the notice explains it. Members can question whether a stated constraint is real while concentrating their advice on choices still open.

items.title: Responsibility
items.body: Advice needs someone able to receive it and respond. Name the decision-making role and the date for its response; if that person cannot act on the recommendation, arrange the proper route before presenting the task.

tabs.label: Too broad
tabs.body: A broad request can surface important concerns, but it leaves members uncertain about priorities and influence. Narrow it to the actual decision and keep a route for issues outside scope rather than silently discarding them.

tabs.label: Too late
tabs.body: Endorsement after release may be useful feedback for a future revision, but it cannot honestly be called influence over the finished choice. Explain that limit and identify whether any remedy or later redesign remains possible.

tabs.label: Usable
tabs.body: An open outreach choice invites practical advice without implying control over the fixed date. Compare methods and their effects, then give members enough context to propose an alternative the team has not considered.

check.question: Which invitation supports useful advice?
check.correct: Compare two outreach approaches before release, with authority and constraints explained.
wrong: Ask one member to predict everyone’s response.
check.feedbackCorrect: Members have a consequential choice and an accurate understanding of their role.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A finished notice can still receive feedback, but it offers no influence over its original release. Unlimited policy authority and one member’s prediction also overstate the council’s role. Look for an open choice, a confirmed remit, and a responsible decision maker.

lessons.summary: Write a brief explaining alternatives and missing evidence.
lessons.objective: Write a brief explaining alternatives and missing evidence.

Separate facts from predictions in an advisory packet.

lessons.statement: A brief should make the decision easier to question.

intro.heading: Prepare a balanced decision brief
intro.body:
Members bring knowledge but may not share a team’s acronyms or background. Put the question first. Present feasible approaches with comparable detail: benefits, burdens, uncertainties, and who may experience them differently. Keep background available without burying the choice.

A letter-only option and a letter with contact choices should not be labeled “practical” and “costly extras.” Those labels settle the argument early. Show what the team actually knows about workload and confusion, and mark predictions as predictions.

Ask how members can review materials. Late delivery may exclude a person who needs accessible preparation even when meeting support is available. If important information arrives late, reconsider whether enough time remains for useful advice.

lessons.keyStatement: A brief should make the decision easier to question.

items.title: Question
items.body: Start the brief with the question in one or two sentences. For the notice, ask which contact approach reduces confusion; provide history afterward. Members should not have to infer the choice from a packet assembled for a different audience.

items.title: Comparison
items.body: Compare the same dimensions for each approach: workload, access, likely effects, and unknowns. Calling the letter-only option practical while describing contact choice only as expensive directs the answer. Balanced comparison can still acknowledge genuine cost differences.

items.title: Preparation
items.body: Preparation is part of participation. Ask about usable formats and allow appropriate review time; a captioned meeting does not repair a packet a person could not read beforehand. If a key option arrives late, coordinate the response instead of assuming attendance means readiness.

tabs.label: Fact
tabs.body: A documented date is a fact about the decision boundary. Explain who confirmed it and whether it applies to this release. Even a fact needs enough context for members to understand its significance.

tabs.label: Prediction
tabs.body: A projected fall in calls may inform planning, but it should not be presented as an observed benefit. Show the basis and uncertainty so the council can ask whether the prediction overlooks new confusion or unmet need.

tabs.label: Gap
tabs.body: A missing usability review affects confidence in the preferred approach. The council may recommend a check before release or a conditional choice; hiding the gap would prevent it from offering that useful advice.

check.question: How should a one-sided packet be repaired?
check.correct: Present comparable alternatives and identify untested predictions.
check.feedbackCorrect: A balanced brief lets members examine both the choice and its evidence.
check.feedbackIncorrect: More pages and acronyms do not fix a one-sided decision brief. Removing uncertainty may make it sound confident while depriving members of a reason to question the choice. Present comparable alternatives and label predictions and missing checks explicitly.

lessons.title: Retain disagreement honestly
lessons.summary: Distinguish silence, individual advice, and a council recommendation.
lessons.objective: Distinguish silence, individual advice, and a council recommendation.
objectives: Distinguish silence, individual advice, and a council recommendation.
Invite reasons behind conflicting proposals without demanding disclosure.
Record unresolved differences without inventing consensus.
takeaways: Do not infer agreement from silence.
Explore reasons without demanding personal stories.
Record the recommendation and its important qualifications.
lessons.statement: Different reasons can reveal a better option.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Retain disagreement honestly
intro.body:
A meeting can sound unanimous when only two people speak. Other members may be considering the issue, waiting for communication support, or choosing not to describe a personal experience. Offer different ways to contribute and follow the council’s own recommendation procedures.

One member may favor telephone follow-up; another may worry that unexpected calls resemble scams. Ask what conditions would help: advance notice, recognizable contact details, or a choice of methods. Neither person should have to prove the concern with a painful story.

Summarize the reasons and invite correction. Record conditions, dissent, and missing evidence. A facilitator’s impression is not a formal recommendation, and a member’s view is not the view of an entire community.

Record unresolved differences without inventing consensus.

lessons.keyStatement: Different reasons can reveal a better option.

items.title: Invite
items.body: Ask what concern lies behind the preference and what would address it. For conflicting views on calls, ask about scam risk and reachable contact methods rather than which member best represents the community. Written input can reveal a perspective missed in rapid discussion.

items.title: Reflect
items.body: Restate each reason and let the speaker correct it. A concern about unexpected calls is not necessarily opposition to all telephone contact. An accurate reflection can reveal a shared condition, such as advance notice, without pretending the original preferences were identical.

items.title: Record
items.body: Use the council’s established method to determine a recommendation. Record a condition or unresolved difference where it affects the decision. A facilitator’s impression that the room is positive cannot replace that process or turn silence into a vote.

tabs.label: Silence
tabs.body: Silence may reflect thought, inaccessible pacing, or a choice not to speak. It can reduce visible conflict, but treating it as consent creates an inaccurate record. Offer a way to contribute and establish the actual recommendation.

tabs.label: Difference
tabs.body: A disagreement can slow the agenda while improving the option. Phone access and scam concerns can both matter; test whether a recognizable contact method or participant choice addresses the reasons before forcing a single preference.

tabs.label: Recommendation
tabs.body: An adopted recommendation provides a decision-relevant account, not proof that every member has the same view. Include the qualifications required by the council’s process so the agency sees where support depends on a condition.

check.question: What should disputed minutes record?
check.correct: The alternatives, reasoning, conditions, and actual recommendation process.
wrong: Unanimous support because no vote occurred.
Each view as a whole community’s position.
check.feedbackCorrect: An accurate record preserves evidence useful for the decision.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A record of unanimous support is attractive because it makes action simpler, but it is false when agreement was not established. Removing a minority concern also loses evidence. Preserve the actual advice, differing reasons, and the council’s recommendation procedure.

items.text: One member requests recognizable caller identification.
A member requests more preparation time.
Members differ about unexpected calls.

responses: Convenience does not justify false agreement.

lessons.title: Respond to advice with reasons
lessons.summary: Connect a recommendation with the decision it influenced.
lessons.objective: Connect a recommendation with the decision it influenced.
objectives: Connect a recommendation with the decision it influenced.
Assign responsibility and a review for conditional advice.
takeaways: Respond to each meaningful part of the advice.
Explain rejection as carefully as adoption.
Do not report planned work as completed.
lessons.statement: A thank-you is not a decision response.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Respond to advice with reasons
intro.body:
A general thank-you acknowledges time but does not show influence. A useful response names the advice, what changed, and why. If contact choice was adopted but a longer deadline was not, explain each result rather than treating the advice as one indivisible request.

Some recommendations will not be adopted. “Not feasible” leaves members unable to tell whether their concern was understood. Identify the real constraint, remaining risk, and any option still being examined.

Do not describe planned work as completed. A promised usability review needs a responsible role, a date, and a return to the council with findings. The response becomes part of the decision, especially when the effects are uncertain.

Explain non-adoption using specific reasons.

lessons.keyStatement: A thank-you is not a decision response.

items.title: Advice
items.body: Restate the recommendation before saying what happened to it. If members asked for contact choice and a review, identify both components. Otherwise adopting one small wording change can be incorrectly reported as accepting the whole recommendation.

items.title: Reason
items.body: Explain the reason at the level of the actual decision. A fixed statutory or authorized deadline is different from an untested staff preference. If a suggestion was rejected, identify the constraint and any remaining risk rather than relying on “not feasible.”

items.title: Follow-through
items.body: Separate completed changes from promised checks. For the notice, identify who will conduct the usability review, when the council will hear back, and what happens if timing changes. That creates a usable commitment rather than an optimistic status.

tabs.label: Courtesy
tabs.body: A thank-you can be respectful and is still insufficient as the only response. Members gave advice to influence a decision; courtesy without the result leaves them unable to judge whether their reasoning was considered.

tabs.label: Vague refusal
tabs.body: A terse refusal saves words but conceals whether the constraint was understood correctly. Give the specific reason and outstanding concern, allowing members to see a possible future option or identify a mistaken assumption.

tabs.label: Traceable response
tabs.body: A traceable response may include partial adoption. Explain how contact choice changed, why the date did not, and when confusion will be checked. This preserves both influence and uncertainty without claiming all concerns are settled.

check.question: Which response closes the loop?
check.correct: State advice, decision, reasons, and review for unresolved concerns.
wrong: Thank members without discussing the decision.
Describe a planned review as completed.
check.feedbackCorrect: Members can see both influence and unfinished responsibilities.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A general thank-you does not show the decision, and saying everything was incorporated exaggerates partial adoption. Describing a planned review as finished creates a second failure. Name the advice, actual action, reason, and unresolved commitment with its owner and date.

items.text: Members requested contact choice.
A member raised scam concerns.
The notice changes its contact explanation.
The confirmed deadline remains for the stated reason.
A lead will examine confusion after release.

move.control: You can connect advice with action and reasons.
move.failure: Members cannot tell whether participation mattered.

lessons.statement: Personal disclosure should not be the cost of improving a process.

intro.heading: Protect people and use the person or area responsible
intro.body:
A member may raise an individual experience because it explains a barrier. Take the concern seriously without inviting identifying case details into a public record. Do not promise confidentiality without checking the relevant rules. Arrange the appropriate route through the program, complaint, accommodation, or legal office.

The general question can remain: Are contact instructions confusing or inaccessible? Remove identifying facts before asking the council to advise on that question. A public discussion is not an eligibility appeal or complaint investigation.

The council can surface concerns without substituting for an office with formal authority. For example, a proposed purchasing change needs the appropriate procurement authority; a public advisory vote cannot approve it.

lessons.keyStatement: Personal disclosure should not be the cost of improving a process.

items.title: Privacy
items.body: Pause identifying detail without dismissing the concern. Explain the appropriate nonpublic route and ask the responsible staff what can be recorded or shared. Mentioning a neighbor’s case does not authorize displaying that person’s file to the council.

items.title: Formal concern
items.body: A complaint or eligibility dispute needs the authorized process. The council may advise on confusing instructions but cannot decide the person’s case. Help connect the concern to the person or area responsible rather than letting a public vote appear to resolve it.

items.title: General issue
items.body: Keep the general barrier visible after removing identifiers. For example, ask whether people can understand the contact route without describing the individual’s service history. This preserves learning while avoiding unnecessary exposure or a false promise of case resolution.

tabs.label: Case
tabs.body: A named case can make an issue vivid but creates privacy and authority risks in public discussion. Arrange the proper route, then identify the design question that can be examined without the person’s private details.

tabs.label: Design
tabs.body: A general question about contact clarity can support useful advice without a case file. It will not resolve the individual dispute, so communicate both the design discussion and the separate referral rather than conflating them.

tabs.label: Authority
tabs.body: A council’s interest in an issue does not grant formal powers. Matters such as individual eligibility, complaints, or procurement decisions need their authorized processes. Advisory input may identify a problem, but it cannot approve a purchase or decide a case outside the council’s role.

check.question: How should an identifying complaint be handled?
check.correct: Pause details, arrange the proper referral, and retain a suitable non-identifying design issue.
wrong: Ask the council to decide eligibility.
check.feedbackCorrect: The response protects the person while preserving a useful advisory question.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Displaying a file or promising absolute confidentiality may seem responsive but creates risks the facilitator cannot settle. A council vote also cannot determine individual eligibility. Pause details, arrange the appropriate referral, and retain a suitable non-identifying design question.

lessons.summary: Trace one recommendation from invitation through response.

lessons.statement: Activity alone does not establish effective advice.

image.caption: Colleagues share information and consider a decision together.

intro.heading: Review influence rather than meeting counts
intro.body:
A council may meet regularly while its advice never reaches the person deciding. Review one actual choice rather than counting meetings. Follow the question, preparation, deliberation, recommendation, decision, and response. Ask where advice could still affect the outcome.

In the notice example, check whether contact advice changed the final explanation, whether the promised review occurred, and whether members received the findings. Missing follow-up is an unknown, not evidence that nobody was confused.

Invite views on the process without scoring members. A useful repair could be earlier materials, a clearer question, or a role responsible for responses. Keep the review proportionate and focused on a dependable advisory relationship, including when final decisions differ from advice.

lessons.keyStatement: Activity alone does not establish effective advice.

items.title: Influence
items.body: Trace advice to the decision record rather than relying on a meeting report. Find where the contact-choice recommendation entered the draft and who acted on it. If no link can be found, record that uncertainty instead of assuming influence.

items.title: Access
items.body: Review preparation and contribution routes as well as attendance. A member who attended but could not review the packet did not have the same opportunity. Ask which step failed and whether the response actually reached people in usable form.

items.title: Repair
items.body: Choose a repair tied to the observed gap. An overdue response needs a responsible person and date; a late packet needs a changed preparation routine. Reviewing whether the repair occurred is more useful than a broad promise to improve engagement.

tabs.label: Activity
tabs.body: Meeting counts show effort and can describe workload, but they do not establish that advice reached an open decision. Use them as activity information alongside a traced recommendation, not as a substitute for influence.

tabs.label: Influence
tabs.body: A documented change provides evidence of influence, while a reasoned non-adoption response can provide evidence of consideration. Neither proves all advice was useful or every concern resolved; keep the conclusion proportionate.

tabs.label: Unknown
tabs.body: When no follow-up occurred, confusion remains unevaluated. Lack of complaints may reflect unknown access to the feedback route. State the missing check and plan it rather than turning silence into a positive finding.

check.question: Which review is most useful?
check.correct: Trace a recommendation, identify a gap, and agree on a repair and review.
check.feedbackCorrect: This examines the advisory process without unsupported conclusions about people.
check.feedbackIncorrect: High attendance is encouraging but says little about influence or follow-through. Silence does not establish success, and ranking members by staff agreement evaluates the wrong thing. Trace a recommendation, identify the actual gap, and review an accountable repair.
